steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on adapting large language models to content moderation through supervised fine-tuning. Cover how content moderation evolved, the limits of discriminative models and of relying on GPT-4, the fine-tuning-with-reasoning-chains approach, and our pipeline and key findings.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Content moderation today: the discriminative paradigm and its limitations
- New challenges (chatbots) and the promise and limits of LLMs like GPT-4
- Supervised fine-tuning of open-source LLMs with moderation reasoning chains
- Our study: pipeline design (weak supervision, deduplication, hallucination correction) and key findings

  - initial attempts: OpenAI uses GPT-4 to optimize rating systems interactively (cite)

  - limits of third-party GPT-4: (1) Compliance Requirements, (2) Cost Considerations, (3) Domain-Specific Knowledge Injection; custom solutions still open research

  - ideal: SFT of LLMs (cite) yields model far more robust than discriminative ones (Sec. 3.3); in practice many design challenges (data engineering, training)
  - first step: large-scale experiments on feasibility; analyze common techniques across pipeline

steps.text:
Content moderation is an essential topic for the modern internet. In the past decade, internet content moderation has changed a lot, going from early manual rule-based strategies to recent fully automated moderation algorithms based on deep learning. Progress in deep learning has made content moderation much more efficient and precise. Current automated content moderation methods usually follow a discriminative paradigm. In this paradigm, large high-quality datasets are annotated manually, and then a discriminative model is trained with supervision for content moderation. As a recent example, OpenAI describes how they build a holistic solution for real-world content moderation based on this paradigm, covering data preparation, model training, and deployment. This paradigm has been very successful in tasks like text and multimodal moderation and has helped businesses cut a lot of costs, but it also has several limitations: (1) Heavy Reliance on Data Annotation Quality, (2) Limited Robustness to Out-of-Distribution Data in Open Environments, and (3) Lack of Interpretability.

These limitations get worse in new scenarios like chatbots. For example, in chatbots there can be malicious users who try to manipulate the system by building inputs that get around content moderation systems, using techniques like code-switching between several languages, emojis, or variant characters. Traditional supervised discriminative approaches clearly can't deal with the dynamic and adversarial nature of these samples just through data or optimization. On the other hand, generative large language models (LLMs) have recently been successful in many complex reasoning and planning tasks, so it is natural to ask whether we can use the broad grounding knowledge, strong language understanding, and logical reasoning abilities of LLMs to make content moderation models more robust and interpretable. The answer is clearly yes, and there have already been some first attempts. One interesting example is OpenAI using GPT-4 to interactively optimize existing content moderation rating systems, to get optimal moderation performance. We also tried this ourselves by designing prompts so that GPT-4 does automatic content moderation on real-world data (see Fig. 2). GPT-4 not only gives reasonable results but can also give a complete auditing process. But for most companies and organizations, relying on third-party GPT-4 models still has big limitations: (1) Compliance Requirements: regulatory and compliance requirements may limit the use of third-party models for content moderation, (2) Cost Considerations, and (3) Domain-Specific Knowledge Injection. Dealing with these limitations and building custom content moderation solutions that meet specific compliance, cost, and domain requirements is still an ongoing area of research and development.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Content moderation is an essential topic for the modern internet. In the past decade, internet content moderation has changed a lot, going from early manual rule-based strategies to recent fully automated moderation algorithms based on deep learning. Progress in deep learning has made content moderation much more efficient and precise. Current automated content moderation methods usually follow a discriminative paradigm. In this paradigm, large high-quality datasets are annotated manually, and then a discriminative model is trained with supervision for content moderation. As a recent example, OpenAI describes how they build a holistic solution for real-world content moderation based on this paradigm, covering data preparation, model training, and deployment. This paradigm has been very successful in tasks like text and multimodal moderation and has helped businesses cut a lot of costs, but it also has several limitations: (1) Heavy Reliance on Data Annotation Quality, (2) Limited Robustness to Out-of-Distribution Data in Open Environments, and (3) Lack of Interpretability.

These limitations get worse in new scenarios like chatbots. For example, in chatbots there can be malicious users who try to manipulate the system by building inputs that get around content moderation systems, using techniques like code-switching between several languages, emojis, or variant characters. Traditional supervised discriminative approaches clearly can't deal with the dynamic and adversarial nature of these samples just through data or optimization. On the other hand, generative large language models (LLMs) have recently been successful in many complex reasoning and planning tasks, so it is natural to ask whether we can use the broad grounding knowledge, strong language understanding, and logical reasoning abilities of LLMs to make content moderation models more robust and interpretable. The answer is clearly yes, and there have already been some first attempts. One interesting example is OpenAI using GPT-4 to interactively optimize existing content moderation rating systems, to get optimal moderation performance. We also tried this ourselves by designing prompts so that GPT-4 does automatic content moderation on real-world data (see Fig. 2). GPT-4 not only gives reasonable results but can also give a complete auditing process. But for most companies and organizations, relying on third-party GPT-4 models still has big limitations: (1) Compliance Requirements: regulatory and compliance requirements may limit the use of third-party models for content moderation, (2) Cost Considerations, and (3) Domain-Specific Knowledge Injection. Dealing with these limitations and building custom content moderation solutions that meet specific compliance, cost, and domain requirements is still an ongoing area of research and development.

One possible technical approach is to build labeled samples together with a moderation process (a moderation reasoning chain) and then do supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on open-source large language models, to align them with the requirements of a specific content moderation task. In recent years this approach has worked in many tasks other than content moderation, like solving math problems and logical reasoning. Researchers have proposed many techniques to improve the final performance of this approach, including data engineering, audit chain reliability assessment, optimization objectives, and more. Whether these techniques work in real-world content moderation still needs to be validated. A related work comes from AWS, where they try to fine-tune large models directly with label information (without the audit reasoning chain). But in our practical experience, this approach has poor out-of-distribution robustness and does not output an interpretable moderation process.

When adapting LLMs to content moderation, the ideal case is to get a model that is much more robust than the previous discriminative-based models (as shown in Sec. 3.3) just by applying supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to LLMs. But actually implementing this simple idea comes with many design challenges. Different design choices, including data engineering and training methods, have a big impact on how the final model performs. In this paper we take a first step by running large-scale experiments to see if it is feasible to apply large language models to content moderation, and we carefully analyze how effective various commonly used techniques are across the whole pipeline. Specifically, for data engineering, we adapt a weak supervision paradigm to lower the cost of manual annotation. Experts annotate the final labels of the samples, and GPT-3.5 & GPT-4 do the more labor-intensive moderation reasoning chain. Unlike many existing works that adapt fully unsupervised paradigms (where all the data is generated by GPT-3.5 & GPT-4), our approach lets us use human-generated golden labels to reflect on the reasoning chain (see the methods section for details). We also use conventional optimization strategies such as data deduplication. During training, we see the common hallucination issues of GPT models when they generate the moderation reasoning chain for production, and these hallucinations can lead to wrong labels. Here we use the weak supervision information to correct the whole process. Applying this whole pipeline to real-world data, we have several key findings: (1) Including reasoning processes during fine-tuning makes the model more robust and effectively overcomes overfitting; (2) Introducing weak supervision can effectively filter out samples with poor reasoning processes, improve the quality of the fine-tuning data, and improve the performance of the fine-tuned model. (3) Fine-tuning LLMs with reasoning processes can effectively overcome overfitting, even when the model is required to output the classification directly without a reasoning process during deployment.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Content moderation is an indispensable topic in the modern internet [1,2]. Over the past decade, internet content moderation has undergone a profound transformation, evolving from early manual rule-based strategies [3] to recent deep learning-based fully automated moderation algorithms [4]. Progress in deep learning technology has significantly improved the efficiency and precision of content moderation. Current automated content moderation methods typically follow a discriminative paradigm [5,6]. This paradigm involves manually annotating extensive, high-quality datasets, followed by supervised training of a discriminative model for content moderation. As a recent example, OpenAI details how they build a holistic solution for real-world content moderation scenarios based on this paradigm, covering data preparation, model training, and deployment [7]. While this paradigm has achieved significant success in tasks such as text and multimodal moderation, and has helped businesses reduce substantial costs, it also has several limitations: (1) Heavy Reliance on Data Annotation Quality, (2) Limited Robustness to Out-of-Distribution Data in Open Environments, and (3) Lack of Interpretability.

These limitations become more pronounced in emerging scenarios like chatbots [8,9]. For instance, in chatbot scenarios, malicious users may attempt to manipulate the system by constructing inputs that bypass content moderation systems, using techniques such as code-switching between multiple languages, emojis, or variant characters. Traditional supervised discriminative approaches are clearly inadequate for addressing the dynamic and adversarial nature of these samples through data or optimization efforts alone [10]. On the other hand, the recent successes of generative large language models (LLMs) in various complex reasoning and planning tasks naturally lead us to consider whether we can leverage the comprehensive grounding knowledge, strong language understanding, and logical reasoning capabilities of LLMs to enhance the robustness and interpretability of content moderation models. The answer is clearly affirmative, and we have already seen some initial attempts and explorations. An interesting case in point is OpenAI's use of GPT-4 to interactively optimize existing content moderation rating systems [4], aiming for optimal moderation performance. We have also made our own efforts by designing prompts that enable GPT-4 to perform automatic content moderation on real-world data (as Fig. 2 shows). GPT-4 not only produces reasonable results but can also provide a complete auditing process. However, for most companies and organizations, relying on third-party GPT-4 models still presents significant limitations: (1) Compliance Requirements: regulatory and compliance requirements may constrain the use of third-party models for content moderation, (2) Cost Considerations, and (3) Domain-Specific Knowledge Injection. Addressing these limitations and developing custom content moderation solutions that meet specific compliance, cost, and domain requirements remains an ongoing area of research and development.

One viable technical approach is to construct labeled samples with an associated moderation process (moderation reasoning chain) and then perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on open-source large language models to align them with the specific requirements of a given content moderation task. In recent years, this approach has proven successful in various tasks beyond content moderation, such as solving mathematical problems and logical reasoning [11,12,13]. Researchers have proposed a variety of techniques to improve the final performance of this approach, including data engineering, audit chain reliability assessment, optimization objectives, and more [14,15,16]. The effectiveness of these techniques in real-world content moderation scenarios still needs validation. A relevant work comes from AWS [17], where they fine-tune large models directly using label information (without the audit reasoning chain). However, in our practical experience, this approach shows poor out-of-distribution robustness and lacks interpretable moderation process outputs.

By adapting LLMs to content moderation, the ideal case is to build a model that is significantly more robust than previous discriminative-based models (as shown in Sec. 3.3) simply by applying supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to LLMs [18,19]. However, the practical implementation of such a straightforward idea is full of design challenges. Various design choices, including data engineering and training methodologies, have a profound impact on the final model's performance. In this paper, we take a first step by conducting large-scale experiments to assess the feasibility of applying large language models to content moderation scenarios, and we carefully analyze the effectiveness of various commonly used techniques throughout the entire pipeline. Specifically, at the data engineering level, we adapt a weak supervision paradigm to reduce the cost of manual annotation: experts annotate the final labels of samples, while GPT-3.5 & GPT-4 handle the more labor-intensive moderation reasoning chain. In contrast to many existing works that adapt fully unsupervised paradigms (where all data is generated by GPT-3.5 & GPT-4), our approach allows us to leverage human-generated golden labels for reflection on the reasoning chain (see the methods section for details). We also incorporate conventional optimization strategies such as data deduplication [20]. During training, we observe common hallucination issues in GPT models when they generate the moderation reasoning chain for production, and these hallucinations can lead to erroneous labels. Here, we leverage weak supervision information to correct the entire process. Applying this pipeline to real-world data, we arrive at several key findings: (1) Incorporating reasoning processes during fine-tuning can enhance the robustness of the model and effectively overcome overfitting; (2) Introducing weak supervision can effectively filter out samples with poor-quality reasoning processes, improve the quality of the fine-tuning data, and enhance the performance of the fine-tuned model. (3) Fine-tuning LLMs with reasoning processes can effectively overcome overfitting, even when the model is required to directly output the classification without a reasoning process during deployment.
